\chapter{Mientras tanto}
\label{ch:es-mientras-tanto}
\hlchaptermodality{536}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say that two things happened at the same time, and that one thing happened as soon as another did.}

Complete the last lesson of chapter 536: I can say that two things happened at the same time, and that one thing happened as soon as another did.

\section[mientras tanto]{mientras tanto — meanwhile, in the meantime}

\label{lesson:ES-C536-mientras-tanto}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for finally, then the Spanish for later.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: mientras tanto}
\textbf{mientras tanto} — \textquotedblleft{}meanwhile, in the meantime\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Mientras tanto, su hermano llamó a la ambulancia.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Meanwhile, his brother called the ambulance.}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{mientras tanto} is built on \emph{mientras} 'while', which is usually traced to Latin \emph{dum interim} 'while meanwhile', and \emph{tanto}, which comes from Latin \emph{tantum} 'so much' (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{mientras tanto}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{mientras tanto}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{mientras tanto}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for finally, then the Spanish for later, then say \emph{mientras tanto} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does mientras tanto mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Meanwhile, in the meantime\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[al mismo tiempo]{al mismo tiempo — at the same time}

\label{lesson:ES-C536-al-mismo-tiempo}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for later, then the Spanish for meanwhile.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: al mismo tiempo}
\textbf{al mismo tiempo} — \textquotedblleft{}at the same time\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Los dos hablaron al mismo tiempo.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{They both spoke at the same time.}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{al mismo tiempo} is built on \emph{mismo}, from spoken Latin \emph{*metipsimus} 'the very same', and \emph{tiempo}, inherited from Latin \emph{tempus} 'time' (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{al mismo tiempo}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{al mismo tiempo}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{al mismo tiempo}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for later, then the Spanish for meanwhile, then say \emph{al mismo tiempo} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does al mismo tiempo mean? (\textquotedblleft{}At the same time\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[a la vez]{a la vez — at once, at the same time}

\label{lesson:ES-C536-a-la-vez}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for meanwhile, then the Spanish for at the same time.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a la vez}
\textbf{a la vez} — \textquotedblleft{}at once, at the same time\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
No puedo hacer dos cosas a la vez.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I can't do two things at once.}
\end{quote}

Close to \emph{al mismo tiempo}, and shorter.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{a la vez} is built on \emph{vez}, which is inherited from Latin \emph{vicem} 'a turn, a change' (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{a la vez}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{a la vez}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{a la vez}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for meanwhile, then the Spanish for at the same time, then say \emph{a la vez} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does a la vez mean? (\textquotedblleft{}At once, at the same time\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[en cuanto]{en cuanto — as soon as}

\label{lesson:ES-C536-en-cuanto}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for at the same time, then the Spanish for at once.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: en cuanto}
\textbf{en cuanto} — \textquotedblleft{}as soon as\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
En cuanto llegó, se fue a dormir.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{As soon as he arrived, he went to bed.}
\end{quote}

About the future it takes the subjunctive: \emph{En cuanto llegues, llámame.}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{en cuanto} is built on \emph{cuanto}, which is inherited from Latin \emph{quantus} 'how great, how much' (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{en cuanto}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{en cuanto}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{en cuanto}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for at the same time, then the Spanish for at once, then say \emph{en cuanto} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does en cuanto mean? (\textquotedblleft{}As soon as\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tan pronto como]{tan pronto como — the moment that, as soon as}

\label{lesson:ES-C536-tan-pronto-como}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for at once, then the Spanish for as soon as.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: tan pronto como}
\textbf{tan pronto como} — \textquotedblleft{}the moment that, as soon as\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Tan pronto como sonó la alarma, salimos.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{As soon as the alarm went off, we went out.}
\end{quote}

The same as \emph{en cuanto}, a little more formal.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{tan pronto como} is built on \emph{tan}, from Latin \emph{tam} 'so', and \emph{pronto}, which comes from Latin \emph{promptus} 'brought forth, ready' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{tan pronto como}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{tan pronto como}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{tan pronto como}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for at once, then the Spanish for as soon as, then say \emph{tan pronto como} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
